title: Relay Towers Down the Valley
story: A mountain valley has a row of radio relay towers, numbered from 0 at the top to the village at the bottom. An alert starts at tower 0 and must reach the last tower. Each tower can forward the alert down the valley, but only so far: tower i can send it to any of the next reach[i] towers.

Some transmitters are weak, and a few are broken (reach[i] = 0), though a broken tower can still receive. Before the storm season, the rescue team wants to know whether an alert from the top can reach the village at all.
task: Write canReachLastTower(reach). From tower i, the alert can go to any tower j with i < j ≤ i + reach[i]. Return true if some chain of forwards takes the alert from tower 0 to tower reach.length - 1, and false otherwise.
With a single tower, the alert is already at the last tower, so return true.

examples.explanation: Tower 0 can reach towers 1, 2 and 3. Tower 2 can reach 3 and 4. Tower 4 reaches 5, the last one. So 0 → 2 → 4 → 5 works. Towers 1 and 3 are broken, but you do not have to use them.
From tower 0 the alert reaches 1 or 2. Tower 1 reaches only 2. Tower 2 is broken. Nothing ever gets past tower 2, so the strong tower 3 never hears the alert.

hints: In the second example, list every tower the alert can possibly reach. Do those towers form a gap-free block starting at 0?

If the alert can reach tower 5, it can also reach towers 1 to 4: any forward that lands beyond them passed over them from somewhere at or before them. So the reachable towers are always a block 0 to far.
Walk the towers from left to right, keeping far, the farthest tower reachable so far. What does it mean if you arrive at a tower i with i > far?
Set far = 0. For each tower i in order: if i > far, the alert can never get here, so return false. Otherwise update far = max(far, i + reach[i]). If you finish the loop, return true.
bruteForce: Explore every chain: from tower 0 try every tower it can reach, then every tower those can reach, and so on, with a search that marks visited towers. Without marking, the number of chains grows exponentially. With marking it is correct, but each tower may look at up to reach[i] others, so it is O(n²) in the worst case: about 50 million steps for 10,000 strong towers.
The search tracks which towers are reachable, one by one. You only need to know how far the reachable block extends.

js: * @param {number[]} reach  how many towers ahead each tower can send to
* @return {boolean} true if the alert can reach the last tower

tests.note: the strong tower at the end does not help
single tower is already the last
longest hop from tower 0 leads to a dead end
zeros are fine if you jump over them
longest hop lands on a broken tower; 0 -> 2 -> 4 works

js: let far = 0; // towers 0..far can all receive the alert
if (i > far) return false; // a gap the alert cannot cross
py: far = 0  # towers 0..far can all receive the alert
return False  # a gap the alert cannot cross
walkthrough: The reachable towers always form one block, starting at tower 0. So instead of tracking a set of towers, track one number: far, the end of that block. Each tower inside the block can push far further.
• Tower 3: 3 > 2. The alert can never get here, so return false.

A common wrong idea is to always forward to the farthest tower. In [2, 3, 0, 0, 1, 0] that sends the alert from 0 to the broken tower 2 and gets stuck, while 0 → 1 → 4 → 5 works. Tracking far avoids choosing a route at all.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, constant work per tower.
solution.takeaway: When the set of reachable positions is always a prefix, replace the set with its right edge. A running "farthest so far" turns a search into a single sweep.
